624.title: The martyrs
624.hook: those tortured and killed who kept their faith and hair to the last breath
624.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the men and women who gave their lives for their faith and kept Sikhi with their hair to the last breath, and gurdwaras and museums often display paintings of these martyrs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: andith, and your line: see, and overlook. Today the Ardas reaches its hardest passage. Let's take it gently.

The Central Sikh Museum, inside the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar, has whole walls of paintings that are hard to look at. Men and women in the middle of terrible suffering, and again and again, the same detail: their faces are calm. Children stop in front of them with their parents, and the parents explain, quietly, who each person was. Those paintings illustrate, almost line by line, one passage of the Ardas: the one that remembers those who died rather than give up their faith.
screen: `WALLS OF HARD PAINTINGS.` → `AGAIN AND AGAIN, A CALM FACE.` → `ONE PASSAGE OF THE ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The passage begins: jinhaan singhaan singhneeaan ne, those Singhs and Singhnis, men and women both, who gave their heads for dharam, for faith and righteousness. Then it names, briefly, what was done to them: cut apart joint by joint, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn in two. Each phrase points to real people Sikhs remember by name. Bhai Mati Das, sawn apart in Delhi at the time of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom. Bhai Mani Singh, cut joint by joint at Lahore. Bhai Taru Singh, who tradition says chose to have his scalp removed rather than cut his hair. The Ardas doesn't linger. It says what happened, plainly, and moves on. Then comes the line that gives today its carry: sikhee kesaan suaasaan naal nibaahee. They kept Sikhi, with their kes, their uncut hair, to the last suaas, the last breath. Nibaahee is the verb from Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok about companions: kou na nibhio saath, no one saw it through. Here the Ardas names the ones who did. And just before: dharam naheen haariaa. They did not lose their faith. Not the fight; many of them lost that. They didn't lose the thing that mattered to them. That's how Sikhs remember martyrs, shaheed: not as victims, but as witnesses. Shaheed is a word Punjabi shares with Arabic, where it carries the sense of a witness. Why say this every day? Sikhs would say: so that no one forgets what was given for them, and so that the small daily choices of faith are held up beside the great ones.
screen: `SINGHS AND SINGHNIS: MEN AND WOMEN.` · `NAMED, PLAINLY, AND NOT LINGERED ON.` · `KEPT SIKHI WITH THEIR HAIR, TO THE END.` · `SHAHEED: A WITNESS.` · then, large: `TO THE LAST BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let your breath slow; you don't need to picture anything painful. For a minute, just hold the fact that people gave everything for what they believed, and that their families still say their names, counting your breaths if it helps: suaas, breath. If you pray, end the silence with Waheguru.
The martyrs. Shaheed, the witnesses: Singhs and Singhnis who did not lose their faith, and kept Sikhi to the last breath.
Your line: to the last breath. They saw it through, all the way. See you tomorrow.

625.title: For the gurdwaras
625.hook: those who gave their lives to keep gurdwaras open and pure
625.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who sacrificed for the service of the gurdwaras, a line many connect with the Gurdwara Reform Movement of 1920 to 1925 and the Nankana Sahib massacre of 1921.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the martyrs, and your line: to the last breath, faith kept all the way through. Today, a phrase in the same passage that points to the twentieth century.

You walk to your gurdwara one morning, the place where your grandparents were married and your children were named, and the man who controls it tells you that people like you aren't welcome. He treats the offerings as his own income. The deeds are in his name. The law, as it stands, is on his side. What do you do? In the early 1920s, in Punjab, tens of thousands of Sikhs faced that question. Their answer cost many of them their lives, and the Ardas still remembers them in one short phrase.
screen: `YOUR GURDWARA, AND YOU'RE NOT WELCOME.` → `THE DEEDS ARE IN HIS NAME.` → `PUNJAB, THE EARLY 1920s.`

segments.voice: Among the ancient tortures in the martyrs' passage comes a phrase that sounds different: gurduaariaan dee sevaa laee kurbaaneeaan keeteeaan. Those who made sacrifices for the service of the gurdwaras. The background: over the 1700s and 1800s, many historic gurdwaras came under hereditary custodians called mahants. Some cared for them faithfully. Others came to treat the shrines as family property, and under British rule the courts often backed them. Some turned away Sikhs from so-called low castes, or allowed practices in the gurdwara that Sikh teaching rejects. Between 1920 and 1925, Sikhs organized to take the gurdwaras back, in the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Its campaigns were called morchas, and many were deliberately nonviolent. The worst day came in February 1921 at Nankana Sahib, Guru Nanak's birthplace. A peaceful group of Sikhs arrived to take over the shrine, and the mahant's armed men attacked them inside. Well over a hundred were killed; sources differ on the number. At Guru ka Bagh in 1922, volunteers walked forward in batches to be beaten by police without raising a hand. The English clergyman C. F. Andrews watched it happen and wrote about it, and reports like his carried the story far beyond Punjab. In 1925 a new law placed the historic gurdwaras of Punjab under an elected Sikh committee, which still manages them. So when Sikhs walk into a gurdwara today and find the doors open to everyone, the langar free, the Guru Granth Sahib honored, they're walking through doors that someone held open. The Ardas asks them never to forget whose hands those were.
screen: `MAHANTS: THE HEREDITARY CUSTODIANS.` · `1920 TO 1925: THE MORCHAS.` · `NANKANA SAHIB, FEBRUARY 1921.` · `DOORS SOMEONE HELD OPEN.` · then, large: `THEY KEPT THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Picture a gurdwara, where anyone may enter, head covered and shoes off, and walk up to it in your mind: the shoe racks, the smell from the langar, the sound of kirtan. Then picture the door itself, and the people who once stood there so that anyone could walk through it. If you pray, say Waheguru at the threshold.
Morcha, a nonviolent campaign: those who gave their lives in the 1920s so the gurdwaras would be open to all, and served as the Gurus taught.
Your line: they kept the doors. Every open door was once held open by someone. That's day six hundred twenty-five.

626.title: The five Takhts
626.hook: the Ardas remembers the five seats of authority and all gurdwaras
626.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the five Takhts and all gurdwaras; hukamnamas for the whole community are issued from the Akal Takht in Amritsar.

segments.voice: Yesterday: morcha, and your line: they kept the doors, held open in the 1920s. Today the Ardas puts five pins in a map.

Draw a map of India and put five pins in it. Two in Punjab, close together. One more in Punjab, farther south. One way out east, on the Ganges, in Bihar. And one deep in the south-center of the country, in Maharashtra, far from all the others. These five pins aren't simply big gurdwaras. They're places where the community's authority sits, and the Ardas names them, as a group, every time it's prayed.
screen: `FIVE PINS IN A MAP OF INDIA.` → `PUNJAB, BIHAR, MAHARASHTRA.` → `WHERE AUTHORITY SITS.`

segments.voice: After the martyrs, the Ardas says: panjaan takhtaan, sarbatt gurduaariaan daa dhiaan dhar ke. Fixing the mind on the five Takhts and all the gurdwaras, say Waheguru. Takht means a throne, the seat of a ruler. A gurdwara is a house of the Guru, where the sangat prays. A Takht is a seat of authority, where decisions for the whole community are made and announced. One is the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, which Guru Hargobind, the Guru of the two swords, built facing the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Edicts called hukamnamas, binding on Sikhs everywhere, are issued from there. The other four are tied to the life of Guru Gobind Singh. Takht Sri Patna Sahib, in Bihar, marks where he was born. Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib, at Anandpur, marks where he founded the Khalsa. Takht Sri Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo in southern Punjab, is where tradition says he stayed for a time and a final edition of the scripture was prepared. And Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, at Nanded in Maharashtra, marks where he died. Then the Ardas widens out: sarbatt gurduaariaan, all the gurdwaras. Every one, from the Harmandir to a rented hall above a shop. Five seats of authority, and every house of the Guru: all held in mind in one breath.
screen: `TAKHT: A THRONE, A SEAT.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT, AMRITSAR.` · `FOUR SEATS FROM THE TENTH GURU'S LIFE.` · `AND ALL THE GURDWARAS.` · then, large: `FIVE SEATS.`

segments.voice: Go through the five slowly in your mind: Akal Takht, Amritsar; Kesgarh Sahib, Anandpur; Damdama Sahib, Talwandi Sabo; Patna Sahib, Bihar; Hazur Sahib, Nanded. Pick one and picture it, the dome, the pilgrims, the morning light, then widen out to every gurdwara, including the one nearest you. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Takht. A throne, a seat of authority: the Akal Takht and four seats from the life of Guru Gobind Singh.
Your line: five seats. One for the Timeless, four from the tenth Guru's life. Day six hundred twenty-six, done.

627.title: The Khalsa's prayer
627.hook: the whole Khalsa asks to remember the Name, and through it all joy
627.howItsDone: The petition part of the Ardas begins with a prayer for the whole Khalsa: that Waheguru come to mind, and through that remembrance every comfort; the word Waheguru is said three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Takht, and your line: five seats. For two weeks the Ardas has been remembering. Today, at last, it starts to ask.

If you were handed one wish for everyone you know, all of them at once, what would you ask for? The usual answers come fast: health, money, safety, maybe peace. Good wishes, all of them. The Ardas has spent its whole first half remembering: the Power, the ten Gurus, the scripture, the five, the four, the forty, the sharers, the martyrs, the Takhts. Now it turns to its first request, made on behalf of the entire community, everywhere in the world. And what it asks for first isn't health, or money, or safety.
screen: `ONE WISH, FOR EVERYONE.` → `HEALTH, MONEY, SAFETY?` → `THE ARDAS'S FIRST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The request begins: prathme sarbatt khaalsaa jee kee ardaas hai jee. First, this is the prayer of the whole Khalsa. Prathme, first, echoes the very first word of the opening stanza, pritham: first, remember the Power. Sarbatt means all, entire, every one. So before anyone asks for themselves, the prayer is said for the whole community. And what does the whole Khalsa ask? In paraphrase: may Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru come into the mind. Chit aave. Chit is the mind, the heart's attention; aave, may it come. The first request is to remember God. Then: chit aavan kaa sadkaa, sarab sukh hove. Sadkaa is a lovely word: by virtue of, as the fruit of. Sarab sukh: all comfort, all happiness. By the grace of that remembering, may there be every joy. Look at the order. Joy isn't asked for directly; it's asked for as the fruit of remembering. Some Sikhs hear the Gurus' whole teaching folded into that one sentence. Health, money and safety come and go, as a month of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks made plain. The Name is what remains. And the word comes three times, in the prayer itself: Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru. It's the sound of a community trying, together, to make the remembering happen even as it asks for it.
screen: `PRATHME: FIRST, FOR THE WHOLE KHALSA.` · `CHIT AAVE: MAY GOD COME TO MIND.` · `SADKAA: AS THE FRUIT OF THAT.` · `SARAB SUKH: EVERY JOY.` · then, large: `THE NAME BRINGS JOY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle, then say Waheguru three times, slowly, the way the Ardas does, leaving space between each. Then simply sit and notice whatever comes after: calm, restlessness, nothing much, all fine. If you don't pray, sit with a word that matters to you instead, and notice what it brings.
Chit, the mind's attention. First, for the whole community: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that remembering, every joy.
Your line: the name brings joy. Remembering comes first, and then the asking. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

628.title: Gifts asked for
628.hook: the gift of Sikhi, of hair, of discipline, discernment, trust and faith
628.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs ask for a string of gifts: Sikhi, kes, rahit, bibek, visaah and bharosaa, each ending in daan, before the greatest gift of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday: chit, and your line: the name brings joy, joy as the fruit of remembering. Today the Ardas makes a list, and it isn't the list you'd expect.

Read a child's birthday wish list and you learn a lot about the child. Read a grown-up's and you learn even more. Usually the list is made of things: a phone, a car, a trip, a bigger kitchen. The Ardas has a wish list too, and it's made of things you can't buy, wrap or hold. Each item ends with the same word, daan, a gift, so that said aloud it has a rhythm, like a steady drumbeat. Six of them come before the last and greatest.
screen: `A WISH LIST SAYS WHO YOU ARE.` → `NOTHING YOU CAN BUY.` → `DAAN, DAAN, DAAN.`

segments.voice: A little further on, the community asks: sikhaan noon sikhee daan, kes daan, rahit daan, bibek daan, visaah daan, bharosaa daan. To the Sikhs, give the gift of Sikhi, of kes, of rahit, of bibek, of visaah, of bharosaa. Daan is a gift, the kind given freely, not earned. Take them in turn. Sikhee daan: the gift of Sikhi itself, the path, the life of a learner. Even being a Sikh is treated as a gift to receive, not an achievement. Kes daan: the gift of uncut hair, which Sikhs keep as the Guru's form. The martyrs kept it to the last breath; here it's asked for as something given. Rahit daan: the gift of discipline, the Sikh way of life kept day after day. Bibek daan: the gift of discernment, telling right from wrong, true from false, especially when it's hard to see. Visaah daan and bharosaa daan: the gift of trust and the gift of faith. They sound alike, and they overlap. One way Sikhs gloss them: visaah as trusting, bharosaa as the confidence to lean your whole weight on God. Both are asked for, side by side, as if one weren't enough. None of these is about circumstances. The Ardas doesn't ask here for an easier life. It asks for the inner equipment to live any life well: discipline, discernment, trust. Ask for faith, the Ardas suggests, and you're asking for something no situation can take.
screen: `DAAN: A GIFT, GIVEN FREELY.` · `SIKHI, KES, RAHIT: THE PATH ITSELF.` · `BIBEK: TELLING TRUE FROM FALSE.` · `VISAAH, BHAROSAA: TRUST AND FAITH.` · then, large: `ASK FOR FAITH.`

segments.voice: Let the six pass slowly through your mind: the path, the form, discipline, discernment, trust, faith, and notice which one you feel the lack of right now; maybe bibek for a decision, bharosaa for a fear, rahit for a habit that's slipped. If you pray, ask for it in the Ardas's own word, daan, a gift; if you don't, hold it as a hope for the day.
Bibek, discernment: one of six daan, alongside Sikhi, kes, rahit, visaah, bharosaa, none of them things you can buy.
Your line: ask for faith. Nothing on this list can be bought or wrapped. That's today, done.

629.title: The greatest gift
629.hook: above all, the gift of the Name
629.howItsDone: At the end of the Ardas's list of gifts, Sikhs ask for daanaan sir daan naam daan, the gift of the Name above all gifts; some also speak of receiving naam at the amrit ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bibek, and your line: ask for faith. That list had six gifts. Today, the seventh, the one at the head of the list.

On some strings of prayer beads, one bead is different from the rest: bigger, or set apart, or with a tassel. You start from it and finish at it, and your fingers know when they've reached it without looking. The Ardas's list of gifts works the same way. Sikhi, kes, rahit, bibek, visaah, bharosaa: six gifts, each one precious. Then one more, marked out from all the others with a single phrase, so that no one could mistake which one matters most.
screen: `ONE BEAD IS DIFFERENT.` → `YOUR FINGERS KNOW IT.` → `ONE GIFT, SET APART.`

segments.voice: After the six gifts, the Ardas says: daanaan sir daan, naam daan. The gift at the head of all gifts: the gift of the Name. Sir is the head, the top, the crown: the gift that crowns the others. Naam, the Name, has come up many times on this path. It isn't only a word for God. It's God's presence, known and remembered, filling a life. Why is it above discipline, discernment, trust and faith? Because, Sikhs would say, it's the source of them. Think back to chit, two days ago: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that, every joy. And Guru Tegh Bahadur's last salok: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The Ardas says the same thing a third way. Of everything that can be given, it names this one to ask for and want most. The word daan has a second edge, too. Here it means a gift received. But Gurbani also groups three words, naam, daan, ishnaan: the Name, giving, and cleansing. There, daan means giving to others. So the Name is a gift you receive, and a life of giving is how it shows. Some Sikhs also speak of the amrit ceremony as receiving naam daan, the gift of the Name, from the Panj Pyare. In a ceremony or in the quiet of a morning, the Ardas asks for it as a gift. In this teaching, nobody earns the Name. They ask for it, and they receive it.

630.title: Kitchen and sword
630.hook: may the kitchen that feeds and the sword that protects both prevail
630.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs ask that wherever the Khalsa is there be protection and grace, and that deg and tegh, the langar's cauldron and the sword, prevail together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: naam daan, and your line: the name above all. Today, two words from eight days ago come back: the pot and the sword.

A huge iron pot, wide enough for a child to sit in, sits on a fire behind a gurdwara, with dal bubbling in it for five hundred people. Then there's a sword, a real one, curved, hanging on the wall of a Sikh home or carried in procession at Vaisakhi. They look like opposites: one for feeding, the other for fighting. And yet the Ardas puts them side by side, in three short words, and asks for both of them to win. Day six hundred twenty-two remembered the people who ran the pot and wielded the sword. Now the Ardas makes those two things a single prayer.
screen: `A POT WIDE ENOUGH FOR A CHILD.` → `A SWORD ON THE WALL.` → `OPPOSITES, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Just before the gifts, the Ardas says: jahaan jahaan khaalsaa jee saahib, tahaan tahaan rachhiaa riaait. In paraphrase: wherever the Khalsa is, there may there be protection and grace. Then three words: deg tegh fateh. Deg is the big cooking cauldron, the pot of the langar. Tegh is the sword. Fateh, from the opening greeting, is victory. May the kitchen and the sword be victorious. The deg stands for feeding: the free kitchen, open to anyone, where everyone sits on the same floor. The tegh stands for protecting: standing up for those who can't stand up for themselves. Sikhs would say they aren't opposites at all, but two ways of caring for people. One keeps them alive; the other keeps them safe. A community that only feeds can't protect the people it feeds. A community that only fights forgets why it fights. So the Ardas asks for both to prevail, together. The phrase is old. Deg, tegh and fateh appear together on Sikh seals and coins from the 1700s on, and the words have been a kind of motto ever since. And the order: deg comes first. The kitchen before the sword, just as in the line about the steadfast: those who shared, ran the pot, and wielded the sword. The Ardas then goes on, in paraphrase: may the honor of the tradition be kept, may the Panth be victorious, may the sword help us, may the Khalsa's word stand high. And then come the gifts.
screen: `WHEREVER THE KHALSA IS: PROTECTION.` · `DEG: THE POT. TEGH: THE SWORD.` · `TWO WAYS OF CARING FOR PEOPLE.` · `THE KITCHEN COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `FEED AND PROTECT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who could use a meal, a snack or a cup of tea, a coworker skipping lunch, a neighbor, a tired parent, and picture handing it to them. Then think of someone who could use protecting, a person being talked over, a kid being picked on, and picture standing next to them. Feeding and protecting, side by side; if you pray, say Waheguru.
Fateh, victory: the pot and the sword, both asked to be victorious together, feeding and protecting, the kitchen first.
Your line: feed and protect. The pot and the sword, and the kitchen first. Day six hundred thirty.
